question.text: Mr. Rohan Mehta donates INR 4,00,000 to a local authority for a family-planning programme (100% deduction, subject to 10% of adjusted gross total income cap). His adjusted gross total income (AGTI) for the year is INR 25,00,000. What is his allowable deduction under Section 80G?

answer.text: INR 4,00,000 — the full donation qualifies for 100% deduction without any cap
INR 2,50,000 — capped at 10% of AGTI; 10% of INR 25 lakh = INR 2.5 lakh, and 100% of that cap is allowed
INR 2,00,000 — 50% of the full donation amount

explanation.text: The Logic: Donations to a local authority for promoting family planning fall under the '100% deduction, subject to 10% of adjusted gross total income' category of Section 80G. The qualifying amount is capped at 10% of AGTI = 10% of INR 25,00,000 = INR 2,50,000. Since the category gives 100% deduction on the qualifying amount, the entire INR 2,50,000 is deductible. The balance INR 1,50,000 of the donation yields no deduction. The Trap: INR 4,00,000 would be right if it were a 'without qualifying limit' 100% category (like PM CARES). INR 2,00,000 and INR 1,25,000 confuse the 50% rule with the 100% rule, or apply 50% on top of the AGTI cap. Cross-Exam Context: V-A (MF Distributor) tests 80G in the context of mutual-fund donations to eligible trusts. X-A/X-B (Investment Adviser) tests 80G planning for HNI clients. XXIII frames the question as how the SIA explains the donor-side flow when auditing the SE's 80G receipt register. Assessor's Pro-Tip: When validating a NPO's 80G receipt register, check that Form 10BE certificates were issued before the 31 May deadline and carry the valid 80G registration number. A lapsed registration invalidates donor deductions retroactively and will show up as a donor complaint during the next AIR cycle.
